title: Your school
hookLine: knowing which school you follow, or finding one

lines: TWO WAYS TO STAND, ONE ROW.
A SCHOOL IS NOT A BUILDING.
cards: Two friends stand shoulder to shoulder in a prayer row. When the imam begins, one folds her hands on her chest. The woman beside her lets her arms hang straight at her sides.
Afterward a newcomer asks which of them did it wrong. They both laugh. Neither, they say: each learned it from her school.

You met this back on day one hundred ten. A school here is not a building. It's a madhhab, a way of reading the Qur'an and the Sunnah that scholars worked through, question by question, and handed on.

teach.b: In a story in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, sent his companions out and told them not to pray the afternoon prayer until they reached a certain place. On the road, the time began to run out.
Some said: he meant hurry, so we pray now. Others said: he said there, so we wait. They did both, and when they told him, he blamed neither group.
Faithful people, reading the same words, can reach different conclusions in good faith.
Among Sunni Muslims the well-known schools are the Hanafi, the Maliki, the Shafi'i and the Hanbali, each named for a teacher: Abu Hanifa, Malik ibn Anas, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal.
Twelver Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school, named for Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, and Ibadi Muslims keep their own. Some follow the school of their family or region, the way you inherit a recipe.
Some choose one through a teacher. In Twelver Shia practice, a believer who isn't a scholar follows a living senior scholar for rulings.

And some Muslims, including some Salafis, prefer not to tie themselves to one school and look at the evidence directly, while others answer that a school is the safer road for anyone who isn't a scholar.
Each side makes its case from the Qur'an and the Sunnah.
On a Tuesday, a school answers small questions. What breaks your wudu. How a traveler shortens prayers.
What to do if you forget a step. The Qur'an tells people who don't know to ask those who do. A school is one way of knowing whom to ask.

how: A Muslim may follow one school of law, a madhhab such as the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali or Ja'fari, often learned through family or a teacher, and look up its rulings for everyday questions of prayer, fasting and purity; some prefer to weigh the evidence without binding themselves to one school.

o: a madhhab, a tested way of reading the sources, named for a teacher
the mosque or Islamic school where you first learned to pray
a sect that splits off and stops praying beside other Muslims

games.q: the schools and their teachers — tap the pairs.

s: a madhhab is a kind of mosque building
a madhhab is a school of law: a way of reading the Qur'an and the Sunnah, handed down by scholars.
the Prophet once blamed neither of two groups who read his words differently
on the road, some companions prayed early and some waited; he blamed neither (Sahih al-Bukhari).
every Muslim agrees that you must stick to one school
some say a school is the safer road; others, including some Salafis, prefer to look at the evidence directly.

games.q: you're one of the companions on the road. you were told to pray the afternoon prayer at a certain place, but the time is running out. what do you do?
games.why: some prayed on the road and some waited until they arrived. when the Prophet heard, he blamed neither group (Sahih al-Bukhari). either first answer is in the story.

practice: Bring to mind one act of worship you do, or have watched someone do, like washing before prayer, and walk through it slowly, step by step. At each step, ask: do I know why it's done this way, or only that it is?
Where you're unsure, stop; if you pray, set the intention to learn that one step properly, and if you don't, just stay with the question.

wordCard.voice: Your school. A madhhab, a tested way of reading the Qur'an and the Sunnah, named for a teacher and handed down. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a school of law, a way of reading the sources handed down by scholars.

carryVoice: Your line: know your school. Every small answer you live by comes from somewhere. Until tomorrow.
